title: What to automate
summary: A macro is a list of steps Excel can repeat for you. It’s worth it for jobs you do the same way, often, and it’s the wrong tool for jobs a formula, a Table or Power Query does better. Macros can’t be undone, so save first.
objectives: Say what a macro is, and spot jobs worth automating.
Choose between a formula, Power Query, a macro and an Office Script for a job.
Turn on the Developer tab and run a macro from the Macros list.
Explain why Undo can’t reverse a macro, and work on a copy.

p: Every morning Arjun exports the day’s orders and does the same things: bold the header, colour it, format the money, add a total, widen the columns. Twenty minutes, every working day, and Farah wants it by ten.
The steps never change; only the data does.
Twenty minutes a day is more than seven hours a month.
One missed step and the report looks careless.
In real life: once sent the orders without the total. Farah phoned before he’d finished his tea.

slides.h: A macro is a recipe card
p: A macro is a list of steps saved under a name. Excel keeps them as VBA code, and runs them all, in order, when you ask. You can record one by doing the steps, or write it.
**VBA** (Visual Basic for Applications) is the language macros are written in.
The **macro recorder** writes VBA while you work.
Macros live in the workbook, so the file type changes to .xlsm.
In real life: can’t write formulas, but she can click a button that says Format orders.

p: Before you automate, count. How long does the job take, how often do you do it, and how long will the macro take to build? A daily twenty-minute job pays back a two-hour macro in a week.
Automate jobs that are **frequent**, **the same every time** and **boring**: those are where mistakes creep in.
One-off jobs aren’t worth it, unless they’re huge.
Count the time to fix it when the data changes, too.
In real life: asked Arjun to automate the year-end report. Once a year, so he made a checklist instead.

lecture.title: The right tool, and the risks

p: Macros aren’t the only way to automate. Formulas recalculate on their own, Power Query cleans and combines data and refreshes, and Office Scripts run in Excel for the web. Pick the simplest tool that does the job.
Formulas calculate; macros **do things**: format, move, save, print, send.
If a formula or a Table can do it, don’t write a macro.
P5 covered Power Query; Module 9 covers Office Scripts.
In real life: replaced a macro that copied totals around with three SUMIFS formulas. Nothing to run any more.

p: When a macro runs, Excel clears the Undo list. Ctrl+Z can’t take back what the macro did, or anything before it. So save before you run a new macro, and test it on a copy.
Undo history is wiped as soon as a macro changes the sheet.
**Save before you run** any macro you haven’t tested.
Keep the raw export untouched; let the macro work on a copy.
In real life: tested his first macro on the live file and lost a morning’s typing. Now he works on a copy.

bad.text: The macro clears the wrong columns. Ctrl+Z does nothing. The data is gone unless you have a saved file.

good.title: Save first, test on a copy
good.text: Save, run, check. If it went wrong, close without saving and open the file again.

p: Macro tools live on the Developer tab, which is hidden at first. File, Options, Customize Ribbon, tick Developer, OK. It stays on.
You need it once per computer.
Developer › **Macros** (Alt+F8) lists the macros you can run.
Developer › **Visual Basic** (Alt+F11) opens the editor where the code lives.
In real life: didn’t have a Developer tab. Two ticks later she had one.

modules.code:
Sub FormatDailyReport()
' Formats the day's orders for Farah: header, numbers, a total row
    With Worksheets("Orders")
        .Range("A1:H1").Font.Bold = True
        .Range("A1:H1").Interior.Color = RGB(221, 235, 247)
        .Range("G2:H13").NumberFormat = "#,##0"
        .Range("A14").Value = "Total"
        .Range("A14").Font.Bold = True
        .Range("H14").Formula = "=SUM(H2:H13)"
        .Range("H14").Font.Bold = True
        .Columns("A:H").AutoFit
    End With
End Sub

points: A **macro** is a set of steps saved under a name, written in **VBA**.
Automate jobs that are **frequent, identical and boring**; use formulas and Power Query when they can do it.
Turn on **Developer** in File › Options › Customize Ribbon; **Macros** (Alt+F8) runs them.
A macro **clears Undo**: save first, test on a copy.
recap.cheat: Frequent + identical = automate; save before you run; Undo can’t undo a macro.

cards.back: A set of steps saved under a name, which Excel runs for you. Stored as **VBA** code.
**Frequent**, **the same every time**, and made of **actions** (format, copy, save, print, email).
Formula: calculate a value. Power Query: clean and combine data that refreshes. Macro: do actions.
**Doesn’t work**: running a macro clears the Undo list. Save first.
